unit.can_do_en: say where I lived and worked before.

brief.situation_en: Aino asks about Maria's life in Brazil.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: Where did you live before Finland?

judge.reason: Only register differences (sä/sinä, Suomee/Suomea); same question.
Brasilias/Brasiliassa and mä/minä are register variants; same statement.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Joo, tosi iso. Siel asuu yli kakskyt miljoonaa ihmistä.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä, todella iso. Siellä asuu yli kaksikymmentä miljoonaa ihmistä.
lines.gloss_en: Yes, really big. Over twenty million people live there.

judge.reason: Joo/kyllä, tosi/todella, kakskyt/kaksikymmentä are register variants; same number (over 20 million).
Only register differences (sä/sinä, siel/siellä); same question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: I was a teacher at a school.

judge.reason: Register variants only; same meaning (I was a teacher at school).

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: And why did you move to Finland?

judge.reason: miks/miksi and sä/sinä are register variants; same question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: My husband got a job here.

judge.reason: Mun mies and minun mieheni both mean 'my husband'; same statement.

forms.why_en: Inessive of 'mikä': here it means 'where', asking about a place.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
asua means to live. -i- marks the past and -t goes with sinä: asuit.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
asua means to live. -i- marks the past and -n goes with minä: asuin.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Means 'city': 'Helsinki is a really beautiful city'.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.
Books write todella. In speech people use tosi, 'really', instead.
Siellä means there. Speech drops the last vowel: siel.
Asua 'to live' doubles its last vowel for 'she': hän asuu. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech shortens kaksikymmentä to kakskyt. Books write kaksikymmentä.
After a number the word takes -a: miljoona becomes miljoonaa.
After a number the word takes -tä: ihminen becomes ihmistä.
The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
Tehdä, to do, in the past tense with -t for 'you': teit.
Olla, to be, in the past tense with -n for 'I': olin.
Adds -na for 'as': opettaja becomes opettajana.
Adds -ssa for 'in': koulu becomes koulussa. Speech drops the end: koulus.
And: joins the coffee and the bun in the order.
Speech drops the last i: miks. Books write miksi.
muuttaa means to move house. In the past, with sinä, it becomes muutit.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books add -ni for 'my': mieheni, with mies changing to miehe-. Speech says mun mies.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to get, to be allowed to
forms.why_en: saada means to get. In the past, for 'he' or 'she', it becomes sai.
Työ becomes töitä after tehdä: tehdä töitä means 'to work'. The vowels change from yö to ö.
täältä means 'from here': saada töitä täältä, 'get work from here'.
